section.title: Warning examples
section.p: This chapter has given us speed. We no longer need to return to the limit definition every time we differentiate. We have rules.
That speed is useful, but it also creates a danger. A rule that is remembered only as a symbol can be used in the wrong place.
The safest way to use derivative rules is to keep asking:
A sum, a product, a quotient, a composition, and an inverse are different constructions. Their derivatives are different because their changes are different.

paragraphs.title: Another quick test
paragraphs.p: The false rule loses the term 2x\sin x and changes the other term. It is not a small error. It is a different derivative.

exercise.title: Why is the derivative of a product not the product of the derivatives?

statement.p: The false rule (fg)'=f'g' forgets the original sizes of the factors. In your own words, why do those sizes matter, and what do the two first-order strips record that the false rule throws away?

hint.p: A small change in the width of a large rectangle adds more area than the same change in a small rectangle. Each factor must change once, weighted by the other factor.

subsection.title: The chain rule needs the order of composition
subsection.p: The chain rule is a rule for functions built in layers. The order of the layers matters.
They use the same two functions, but in different orders.

exercise.title: Why does mixing composition order produce the wrong derivative?

statement.p: The functions \sin(x^2) and (\sin x)^2 use the same pieces in different orders, so their derivatives are different. In your own words, why must the outside derivative be evaluated at the inside value, and what common wrong answer comes from swapping the layers?

hint.p: Differentiate from the outside inward, but keep the original construction. The wrong answer 2\sin x\cos x belongs to a different function.

The geometry explains the algebra. The graph of y=x^3 has a horizontal tangent at the origin. Reflecting across the line y=x turns that horizontal tangent into a vertical tangent. A vertical tangent does not have a finite slope as a function y=g(x).

warning.title: Inverse warning
warning.p: An inverse may exist even when the inverse derivative formula cannot be used. If the original tangent is horizontal, the inverse tangent may be vertical.

exercise.title: Why can an inverse exist without a finite inverse derivative?

statement.p: The cube function has an inverse, but the inverse derivative formula would divide by f'(0)=0. In your own words, why is that condition not decorative, and what does a flattened original tangent become after reflection?

hint.p: If the original function does not change to first order, reversing it may create an infinite slope. A horizontal tangent reflects into a vertical tangent.

subsection.title: A rule checklist
subsection.p: When a derivative gets complicated, do not start by writing symbols quickly. Start by reading the structure.

md.mrow: \begin{array}{l} \text{1. Is this built by addition, multiplication, division, or composition?}
\text{2. If it is a composition, what is the inside function?}
\text{3. If it is a product or quotient, have all factors been differentiated correctly?}
\text{4. If it is an inverse or logarithm, are the domain conditions satisfied?}
\text{5. Does the final answer have the right rough behavior and units?} \end{array}

subsection.p: A derivative formula is not only an answer. It is a record of how the function was built.
